Rat Wranglers · ECE 449 · Sensors and Sensor Interface Design

Pest Detection and Humane Deterrence System

A solar-powered field system for organic farms that combines low-power motion sensing, camera-based pest classification, Wi-Fi communication, and targeted light, sound, and motion deterrence.

2-stagePIR trigger, then camera + ML
360°Four PIR sensors around enclosure
600+Images in the custom pest dataset
38 lbMeasured assembled system weight

Project Overview

Problem and Goal

Organic farms have limited options for responding to larger pests without using pesticides or harming animals. The project built an energy-conscious system that detects a possible pest, classifies the camera image, logs the event, and activates a deterrent only after a positive detection.

Integrated System

A Raspberry Pi 4B handles sensor polling, cameras, image processing, and YOLOv8 inference. A Wi-Fi message connects it to a separate deterrence subsystem built around an ESP8266MOD HTTP server and an Arduino Mega 2560. A 12 V, 25 Ah LiFePO4 battery with a solar panel supplies the system.

Targeted, Non-Harmful Response

The deterrence subsystem combines lights, sound, and a moving scarecrow carried by a zipline. The design goal was to discourage pests while avoiding harm to animals and reducing unnecessary power use.

Two-Stage Detection

The system keeps the camera and machine-learning workload idle until a low-power sensor detects movement. A positive image classification then triggers a wireless request to the deterrence unit.

Low-Level PIR Trigger

Four Adafruit PIR sensors sit at 90-degree intervals around the enclosure. Each has an approximately 120-degree sensing arc and a reported range of 20 feet. The Raspberry Pi polls their digital GPIO outputs and activates only the camera paired with the triggered sensor.

Camera Capture

Four 12 MP Arducam IMX708 modules, each with a 120-degree field of view, are mounted above the PIR sensors. At night, the detection system can request a brief light activation to illuminate the scene for the photograph.

YOLOv8 Classification

A lightweight YOLOv8 model runs locally on the Raspberry Pi. The custom dataset contains more than 600 images captured in the lab, around campus, and on the farm, with varied distances, viewpoints, and backgrounds. The trained classes are raccoon, squirrel, and groundhog.

Detection Decision

Inference uses a minimum confidence threshold of 0.25. If the model detects a target pest above the threshold, the Pi sends a Wi-Fi request to activate deterrence; otherwise, the system returns to monitoring the PIR sensors.

Wireless Deterrence Subsystem

Communication and Control

The ESP8266MOD receives HTTP GET requests for full deterrence or a lights-only flash. It signals the Arduino Mega 2560, which coordinates the outputs using non-blocking timing so sound, light, and motion can operate together.

Sound

An SD-card audio track is played by the Arduino and amplified by a 12 V Adafruit MAX9744 Class D amplifier, then sent to a waterproof speaker in a custom 3D-printed holder.

Lights

Two LED flood lights are switched by an N-channel MOSFET and flyback diode. The lights can support nighttime camera capture and can also be activated as part of the deterrence response.

Moving Scarecrow

A DC motor drives a motion line that carries a scarecrow along a zipline between two posts. A separate static load line supports the trolley. Limit switches at the ends of travel signal the Arduino to reverse the motor.

The detection and deterrence units are modular and share the 12 V battery supply. Deutsch connectors were used to make subsystem and peripheral connections easier to assemble and service in the field.

System Tests and Results

The final report compared the prototype with its design criteria. Results show strong photo logging and deterrence performance, alongside gaps in pest classification, field connectivity, and setup simplicity.

Deterrence Feedback

Five evaluators rated the deterrence response 4.8 / 5 for perceived scariness. The moving scarecrow traveled along an approximately 14-foot zipline at about 5 mph.

Cost

The report lists $350.27 for the project build and $483.31 as the estimated cost to reproduce the system. The higher reproduction estimate highlights the difference between a prototype build and a repeatable product bill of materials.

Engineering Challenges and Lessons

Power Integrity

Regulator failures and Raspberry Pi power sensitivity led the team to revise its power approach and use USB-C power for more reliable operation. Safe shutdown handling was added to reduce SD-card corruption during field use.

Field Connectivity

Wi-Fi performance was less reliable in the farm environment than during controlled testing. The report identifies a more reliable communication module as a priority for reducing detection-to- deterrence delay.

Serviceability

As wiring grew, connectors made the system easier to modularize than a single soldered board or loose breadboard. The report also documents a field short caused by crossed connector pins, underscoring the need for keyed, verified connections.

Installation

The zipline gave the scarecrow a large motion area, but the posts, limit switches, speaker, and attachments took time to assemble in the field. Simplifying installation was identified as a key improvement.
